/-!
# Conjecture 5.25

by V. M. Kopytov

Prove that the factor-group of any soluble linearly ordered group by its
derived subgroup is non-periodic.

Here a *linearly ordered group* is a group equipped with a linear (total)
order that is invariant under multiplication on the left and on the right.
The *derived subgroup* of $G$ is the commutator subgroup $G' = [G, G]$, and a
group is *periodic* if every element has finite order.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

    [IsSolvable G] [Nontrivial G] :
    ¬ Monoid.IsTorsion (G ⧸ commutator G) := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
Let $G$ be a nontrivial soluble group with a linear order that is invariant
under left and right multiplication. Then the factor group $G / G'$ of $G$
by its derived subgroup $G' = [G, G]$ is non-periodic, i.e. it contains an
element of infinite order.

The trivial group is excluded: its factor group by its derived subgroup is
trivial, hence periodic.

claims.decomposer_note: Universally quantified over all soluble (solvable) bi-ordered groups G (total order invariant under left and right multiplication); 'non-periodic' means G/[G,G] is not a torsion group, i.e. has an element of infinite order; the trivial group must implicitly be excluded (G nontrivial) since its abelianization is trivial and hence periodic.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same proposition: for every nontrivial solvable group G with a LinearOrder that is left- and right-invariant (MulLeftMono G, MulRightMono G — with Group this yields strict bi-invariance, checked via inferInstance), ¬ Monoid.IsTorsion (G ⧸ commutator G) (= Abelianization G by rfl). Verified in Lean: Monoid.IsTorsion = every element has finite order, so the negation is 'has an element of infinite order' = non-periodic; IsSolvable = derived series reaches ⊥; the hypotheses are satisfiable (Multiplicative ℤ), so the statement is non-vacuous; the trivial group would make the claim false, so [Nontrivial G] is a necessary domain restriction, explained in the docstring. c04 chosen for style: explicit (G : Type*) argument, literal `G ⧸ commutator G` matching 'factor-group by its derived subgroup', AMS 6 20 (ordered algebraic structures + group theory), and docstrings that define the bi-invariant order and justify the nontriviality hypothesis. Compiles with only the sorry warning.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 5.25

by V. M. Kopytov

Prove that the factor-group of any soluble linearly ordered group by its
derived subgroup is non-periodic.

Here a *linearly ordered group* is a group equipped with a linear (total)
order that is invariant under multiplication on the left and on the right.
The *derived subgroup* of $G$ is the commutator subgroup $G' = [G, G]$, and a
group is *periodic* if every element has finite order.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«5.25»

/--
Let $G$ be a nontrivial soluble group with a linear order that is invariant
under left and right multiplication. Then the factor group $G / G'$ of $G$
by its derived subgroup $G' = [G, G]$ is non-periodic, i.e. it contains an
element of infinite order.

The trivial group is excluded: its factor group by its derived subgroup is
trivial, hence periodic.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 6 20]
theorem kourovka.«5.25» (G : Type*) [Group G] [LinearOrder G] [MulLeftMono G] [MulRightMono G]
    [IsSolvable G] [Nontrivial G] :
    ¬ Monoid.IsTorsion (G ⧸ commutator G) := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«5.25»

items: 'Linearly ordered group' is modeled as a group with a LinearOrder that is both left- and right-invariant, via Mathlib's unbundled classes MulLeftMono G and MulRightMono G (bi-ordered group). Mathlib's bundled IsOrderedMonoid / IsOrderedCancelMonoid require CommMonoid and so cannot be used for a general (non-commutative) group. In a group, monotonicity of translations is equivalent to strict monotonicity, so using the Mono (≤) versions loses nothing.
'Derived subgroup' is Mathlib's `commutator G` (= ⁅⊤, ⊤⁆); the factor group is written literally as `G ⧸ commutator G` (definitionally equal to `Abelianization G`).
'Non-periodic' is `¬ Monoid.IsTorsion (G ⧸ commutator G)`, i.e. the quotient has an element of infinite order.

The trivial group is excluded with `[Nontrivial G]` (as prescribed by the decomposition table): it satisfies every other hypothesis but its abelianization is trivial, hence periodic, which would make the statement false as stated. The hypotheses are non-vacuous (e.g. ℤ).
The statement is imperative ('Prove that ...'), not a yes/no question, so it is stated directly as a theorem without `answer(sorry)`.
AMS tags 6 (ordered algebraic structures) and 20 (group theory).

reviewer_notes: Interpretation: 'linearly ordered group' in Kopytov's (Kokorin–Kopytov) terminology is a totally ordered group with two-sided invariant order; the one-sided (right-ordered) reading was not used by any candidate and does not match the source terminology. 'Non-periodic' = not a torsion group. The trivial group is excluded via [Nontrivial G] (its abelianization is trivial hence periodic); since bi-ordered groups are torsion-free this is equivalent to G infinite. The problem is imperative ('Prove that…'), so plain `theorem : P` style is used rather than answer(sorry). No candidate omitted the slot; all were faithful and compiled, differing only in style (Type vs Type*, Abelianization G vs G ⧸ commutator G, AMS 20 vs AMS 6 20, instance-argument vs → form). c06 used an implicit {G : Type*} which is unidiomatic; c04's explicit argument form was preferred.
